newsitem.title: USA: Gore calls House immigrant bill "un-American".
newsitem.headline: Gore calls House immigrant bill "un-American".

text.p: Vice President Al Gore lashed out Thursday at a Republican plan limiting disability aid for legal immigrants, saying it violates the balanced budget agreement and "is un-American."

Representative Clay Shaw, subcommittee chairman, called the Republican plan more fair than that spelled out in the budget agreement and asked Gore to "stick to the facts." But Gore said the Republican approach, particularly a bill approved by the House Ways and Means Committee, "is simply wrong."
"Immigrants have helped to build our entire country. That's been true throughout our entire history," he said in remarks at the Old Executive Office Building, adjacent to the White House.

"The Republican plan, particularly as it currently stands in the House, breaks faith with the bi-partisan balanced budget agreement. But even more, because it treats immigrants who are in this country legally in the most hard and unfair ways, it fails to realise the United States of America is a strong nation because we are a diverse nation," he said.
"The Republican plan as it currently stands is simply wrong. If I can use a sometimes explosive term, in my opinion, the Republican plan is un-American, simply un-American."
Gore added: "It is unworthy of a nation of immigrants and it must be changed."
The political clash centres on efforts in the White House and Congress to change language in the 1996 welfare law that ends federal benefits to most legal immigrants this summer.

The balanced budget deal between Clinton and Republican leaders includes language that legal immigrants who were in the United States by Aug. 22, 1996, and were either on the rolls because of disability or became disabled in the future could receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid.
"We are endeavouring to get the leadership to keep their word," said Gore, adding: "Let's ... do right by the legal immigrants in America."

Shaw, chairman of the human resources subcommittee of the Ways and Means panel, responded to Gore's charges by issuing a letter saying the Republican plan was "more fair and more humane than the approach in the budget agreement."

He also accused Gore of resorting to inflamatory rhetoric in his attack, rather than trying to conduct a calm debate. "If you disagree with our position on benefits for noncitizens," Shaw said, "I suggest that we stick to facts and not try to batter each other with rhetoric."
